title: A discursive essay
subtitle: A question examined, not won
goal: You can examine a contested question at length: frame it precisely, develop competing positions on their strongest form, and arrive at a qualified position of your own.
why: At C1 the examiner is looking for control of qualification: which parts of your claim are strong, which are provisional, and whether you know the difference.
example: Aliya's essay on automation defined 'work' before arguing about it. Her tutor's comment: 'the definition does the arguing'.
writeTask: Write a discursive essay (280–320 words) on whether automation threatens employment: define the terms, develop the strongest case on each side, identify what the disagreement actually turns on, and give a qualified conclusion.

tasks.title: Build the sentence
tasks.howto: Tap the words in the right order — they move into the line. Tap a word in the line to send it back. English word order is fixed, so the order itself carries the meaning.

items.src: I think the second argument is weaker.
answers: The second argument is the weaker of the two.
items.why: At C1 the judgement carries itself; the first person adds nothing.

items.src: The government failed to regulate the sector, and this led to the crisis.
answers: The government's failure to regulate the sector precipitated the crisis.
items.why: Nominalisation is what makes advanced prose dense rather than merely long.

answers: Remote work appears to disadvantage junior staff in their first year.
items.why: Naming the scope makes a claim defensible instead of merely bold.

items.src: The ending of the novel is a bit disappointing.
answers: The novel's ending resolves too neatly for the questions it has raised.
items.why: Say what the flaw is, not how you feel about it.

items.src: They should stop cutting the budget.
answers: Further reductions to the budget should be suspended.
items.why: The passive recommendation depersonalises the demand.

items.cue: Merge two claims with a semicolon
items.src: The data are consistent. The interpretation is not.
answers: The data are consistent; the interpretation offered for them is not.
items.why: A semicolon holds two clauses in balance where a full stop would break them.

items.src: The study is useful. Its sample is too small.
answers: For all its usefulness, the study rests on too small a sample.
items.why: For all its X concedes and criticises in a single clause.

items.src: The committee has rarely acted so quickly.
answers: Rarely has the committee acted so quickly.
items.why: Fronting a negative adverb and inverting is a marker of C1 control.

tasks.title: Rewrite it

items.before: The reform widened access to universities.
items.after: , it did nothing to improve completion rates.
items.why: Conversely reverses the direction of the argument rather than merely opposing it.

items.before: The author documents the problem in detail.
items.after: , the remedies she proposes occupy two pages.
items.why: The imbalance between diagnosis and cure is the criticism.

items.after: , the conclusion has been repeated as settled fact.

items.why: The reversal is what gives a critical review its edge.

items.after: , it postponed every measure that carried a cost.
items.why: Tellingly instructs the reader how to read the fact that follows.

items.ctx: A note to a friend who is also a colleague
items.a: It would be most agreeable to meet at your convenience.
items.why: Register follows the relationship, not the medium.

items.ctx: A letter of complaint with justification
items.a: The response I received did not address the substance of my complaint.
items.b: Your answer completely missed the point.
items.why: Restraint is what makes a formal complaint difficult to dismiss.

items.a: The argument is elegantly framed but thinly evidenced.
items.b: The argument sounds great but there's not much proof.

items.a: One might posit that the sample is unrepresentative.
items.b: The sample looks unrepresentative to me.
items.why: 'One might posit' in a peer discussion is pastiche, not register.

items.a: The author's central claim is that attention is a finite resource.
items.b: Basically the author says we only have so much attention.
items.why: A summary reproduces the claim in the register of the original.

items.ctx: An email to a close friend
items.a: I trust you will find the enclosed of interest.
items.b: Thought you'd like this — have a look.
items.why: Business formulas between friends read as parody.

items.ctx: A message to a colleague you know well
items.a: I should be grateful if you would forward the file at your earliest convenience.
items.b: Could you send the file today?
items.why: Excessive formality between peers reads as irony or as distance.

tasks.title: Who are you writing to?
tasks.howto: The same idea, two versions. Choose the one that fits the reader. Register is not about being polite — it is about distance.

rules.msg: The thesis may open the text, but the recommendation cannot: it has to be earned by the evidence between them.
A conclusion that introduces evidence admits that the body of the text was incomplete.
